title: Relative inertia and the second diagonal of an algebraic-stack morphism
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme], in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention], and let $h:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a morphism of algebraic stacks over $S$ [def-sfb-algebraic-moduli-stack]. Fibred groupoids, morphisms, 2-morphisms and 2-fibre products use [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids], and algebraic spaces use [def-trf-algebraic-space]. The relative inertia $I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}$ has over an $S$-scheme $T$ objects $(x,\alpha)$, where $x\in\mathcal X(T)$ and $\alpha\in\operatorname{Aut}(x)$ satisfies $h(\alpha)=\mathrm{id}_{h(x)}$; arrows $v:(x,\alpha)\to(x',\alpha')$ satisfy $v\alpha=\alpha'v$. Its projection $p$ forgets $\alpha$, and its neutral section $e$ sends $x$ to $(x,\mathrm{id}_x)$. Then $\Delta_h:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ is representable by algebraic spaces. The relative inertia is an algebraic stack, and $p:I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}\to\mathcal X$ is representable by algebraic spaces. There is an equivalence over $\mathcal X$ between $\mathcal X\times_{(\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X)}\mathcal X$, formed using $\Delta_h$ on both sides, and $I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}$; under this equivalence the second diagonal $\Delta_{\Delta_h}$ is the neutral section $e$. For $\mathcal Y=S$, the relative inertia is the absolute inertia $I_{\mathcal X}$.

proof.text: Put $B=\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ and $D=\mathcal X\times_{\Delta_h,B,\Delta_h}\mathcal X$. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-stack-fibre-products] first to $h,h$ and then to $\Delta_h,\Delta_h$. All three stacks in each application are algebraic: in the second application the base is $B$, already obtained in the first. Thus $B$ and $D$ are algebraic stacks. By [lem-sfb-stack-relative-diagonal-finite-type], $\Delta_h$ is representable by algebraic spaces. Only its representability clause is needed.

source.place: Tags 04XS (lemma-properties-diagonal), part (1), and 050Q (lemma-inertia), proof; algebraic.tex Tag 04T2 (lemma-2-fibre-product).

proof.text: Unpack [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids] fibrewise. An object of $D(T)$ is $(x,y,(i,k))$, where $i,k:x\xrightarrow{\sim}y$ and $h(i)=h(k)$. An arrow to $(z,w,(l,m))$ is a pair $(u:x\to z,v:y\to w)$ satisfying $vi=lu$ and $vk=mu$. Define $F:D\to I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}$ by $F(x,y,(i,k))=(x,k^{-1}i)$ and $F(u,v)=u$. Here $h(k^{-1}i)=h(k)^{-1}h(i)=1$, and $u k^{-1}i=m^{-1}v i=m^{-1}l u$, exactly the inertia-arrow condition. Identities and compositions are preserved because $F$ selects the first component. Conversely define $G(x,\alpha)=(x,x,(\alpha,1_x))$ and $G(u)=(u,u)$. The equalities $h(\alpha)=1$ and $u\alpha=\beta u$ give respectively its object and arrow conditions. Both formulas commute with pullback, using the canonical comparison isomorphisms of the fibred categories, since functors preserve identities, composition and inverses. Thus these are morphisms over $S$-schemes, not just unrelated fibre functors.

source.place: Tag 034H (lemma-inertia-fibred-category), explicit functors in the proof.

proof.text: The composite $FG$ is the identity. At $d=(x,y,(i,k))$, the pair $(1_x,k)$ is an isomorphism $GF(d)=(x,x,(k^{-1}i,1_x))\to d$: its two required equations are $k(k^{-1}i)=i$ and $k1_x=k$. For an arrow $(u,v):d\to d^{\prime}$ with second structural isomorphism $m$ at $d^{\prime}$, naturality is the componentwise equality $(u,v)(1_x,k)=(u,vk)=(u,mu)=(1_z,m)(u,u)$. These isomorphisms also commute with pullback, by the same identity/composition formulas. Hence $F$ and $G$ are quasi-inverse equivalences of fibred groupoids. If $q_1:D\to\mathcal X$ is the first projection, $pF=q_1$ and $q_1G=p$ on objects and arrows; the displayed comparison has first component the identity. The equivalence is therefore over $\mathcal X$. This expands the omitted details of the source without invoking a separate inertia-equivalence lemma.

source.place: Tag 034H (lemma-inertia-fibred-category), quasi-inverse and natural isomorphism in the proof.

proof.text: The second diagonal sends $x$ to $(x,x,(1_x,1_x))$ and an arrow $u$ to $(u,u)$. Applying $F$ gives $(x,1_x)$ and $u$, so $F\Delta_{\Delta_h}=e$, including its action on arrows. If $\mathcal Y=S$ is the discrete fibred groupoid represented by the base scheme, $h(\alpha)=1$ for every automorphism over a fixed $S$-scheme. The relative inertia objects and arrows are then exactly the absolute inertia objects and arrows, with the same pullbacks, projection and neutral section.

source.place: section-higher-diagonals, identification immediately before Tag 0CL0 (lemma-diagonal-diagonal); Tag 050Q (lemma-inertia), absolute case.

proof.text: The first projection $q_1:D\to\mathcal X$ is the $2$-base change of $\Delta_h:\mathcal X\to B$ along the other $\Delta_h:\mathcal X\to B$. Its representability follows from step 1 and [lem-sfb-fibred-groupoid-representable-smooth-calculus]. For any scheme $T\to\mathcal X$, the explicit equivalence of step 3 gives an equivalence over $T$ between $I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}\times_{\mathcal X}T$ and $D\times_{q_1,\mathcal X}T$: apply $F$ or $G$ on its first component and retain the structural isomorphism to the fixed object of $\mathcal X(T)$. The latter fibre product is an algebraic space. Being equivalent to an algebraic space is precisely the scheme-test definition of representability in [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. Thus the actual projection $p$ is representable by algebraic spaces.

Finally check algebraicity on the explicit equivalence of step 3, using [def-sfb-algebraic-moduli-stack]. Isomorphism sheaves and descent data for inertia correspond through $G$ to those for $D$, and full faithfulness gives unique corresponding arrows; a descended object of $D$ is sent back by $F$. Hence inertia is an etale stack. A scheme test of its diagonal is equivalent, by $G$ on the two objects and arrows, to the corresponding scheme test of the diagonal of $D$, so it is an algebraic space. Choose a smooth surjective scheme atlas $U\to D$, whose existence follows from step 1. Compose with $F$ to get $U\to I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}$. For each scheme $T\to I_{\mathcal X/\mathcal Y}$ its base change is equivalent over $T$ to $U\times_D T$, with $T\to D$ obtained by $G$ and the comparison $GF\cong1_D$ of step 3. Thus it has exactly the same algebraic-space presentation and smooth surjective projection to $T$. This is a smooth surjective scheme atlas for inertia, proving that inertia is algebraic.
